headline: Texas Lt. Gov.-elect Goodwin puts THC regulation among top 30 bills
dek: Vikki Goodwin says regulating THC is on her reserved list of 30 priority Senate bills, while agriculture commissioner-elect Clayton Tucker calls hemp a lifeline.
key_points: Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin told KSAT-TV she has reserved the first 30 Senate bill numbers for her priorities, and regulating THC is on the list.
Goodwin said she is open to any approach, including full legalization, and is not interested in a full ban on THC.
Agriculture commissioner-elect Clayton Tucker said hemp could be the state's saving grace for farmers in drier western regions.
Republican Rep. Wes Virdell said cannabis is an area where he and Democrats can align, pointing to bipartisan House bills in 2027.
body: Texas's next lieutenant governor has moved THC from campaign theme to legislative priority. Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin told KSAT-TV on Wednesday, 11 November, that she has reserved the first 30 Senate bill numbers for proposals she considers priorities, and that regulating THC is among them, according to Marijuana Moment.

As presiding officer of the Senate, Goodwin will not file bills herself. But low bill numbers are a strong signal in Austin: they mark the measures the Senate's leader wants to move first. That puts THC policy near the front of the 2027 session, a sharp turn from the past two years, when the same office led the push to ban hemp THC products.
## What Goodwin is and is not promising

Goodwin did not commit to a specific model. Asked whether she wants full legalization or a narrower law covering certain hemp-derived THC products, she said officials need more conversations, and asked aloud whether Florida or Oklahoma has the better plan. She said her bottom-line goal is that people can buy safe products, and that she had heard from many veterans who use hemp and THC products for pain.

She said she is open to any approach, including full legalization, arguing that prohibition pushes people to an illicit market where products may be unsafe or laced with fentanyl. At a press conference on Tuesday, 10 November, she said Texas needs regulation around THC and that she is not interested in a full ban.
> Texas has gone from the state most likely to ban hemp THC to one where the Senate's presiding officer lists regulating it as a top-30 priority, in a single election.

The incoming agriculture commissioner is making the same case from the farm side. Clayton Tucker told The Texas Standard, in an interview published on 11 November, that hemp could be the state's saving grace for farmers. He described the crop as very drought-tolerant and well suited to drier western parts of the state, and raised hemp diesel as a possible backup fuel source.

Tucker said his office would make it easier for farmers to grow hemp, and that his main condition is preventing corporate monopolies from forming. That matters for how any THC law is written: licence caps and vertical integration rules decide whether a market is open to small farms or dominated by a few large companies.
## Republicans signal room for a deal

Democrats do not control everything. Republican Rep. Wes Virdell of Kerrville told KXAN-TV that cannabis is an issue where he and Democrats can definitely align, and that he expects very bipartisan bills from the House and hopefully the Senate. He said he wants proper rules on purchase age and product quality, and argued that people are getting felonies for things that do not deserve that classification, such as THC gummies or vape cartridges.

Virdell said he voted for last session's THC ban because outgoing Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick had promised him a major expansion of the state's medical programme, which he now doubts was intended. He later urged Gov. Greg Abbott's team to veto the bill, and Abbott did.

The veto did not end the fight. State agencies then adopted restrictive rules that effectively banned many hemp products, and those rules are being challenged in court, according to Marijuana Moment. As we reported on 8 November, Texas's 15th Court of Appeals cancelled its 8 December hearing on the hemp rules after voters replaced all three of its justices, so a new bench that starts in January will hear the case.

The incoming leadership already has bills to work with. As we reported on 10 November, Democrats have prefiled bills to legalize marijuana for the 2027 session, alongside proposals to expand medical access. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she would like voters to decide on legalization by referendum, which under Texas law would require the legislature to place a constitutional amendment on the ballot.

The open choice is the model. One path is a regulated hemp THC market with age limits, testing and licensing, which would protect the existing retail sector. Another is full adult-use legalization, which would create a new licensed cannabis industry. Goodwin's reference to Florida, a medical-only market built on a small number of vertically integrated licensees, and Oklahoma, a medical market known for its large number of licensed businesses, shows how wide the range still is.

Watch which bills receive Goodwin's reserved low numbers when the legislature convenes in January, and whether the House and Senate converge on a hemp-regulation bill, an adult-use bill or both. Also watch the court challenge to the agency rules, which could reshape the hemp market before lawmakers act, and whether Republican lawmakers like Virdell sign on as co-authors.
